report:
## Conclusion

The claim that consuming more olive oil reduces the risk of stroke is **moderately supported by evidence**, though results vary by population and study design.

**Supporting evidence:**
- A 2021 analysis of Spanish cohorts found that higher olive oil consumption was associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and stroke, with maximum benefit at 20–30 g/day ([Clinical Nutrition, 2021](https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614(21)00503-3/fulltext)).
- A French study of older adults found that higher olive oil use and plasma oleic acid were associated with lower stroke incidence ([Neurology, 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21676914/)).
- An umbrella review concluded that high olive oil consumption significantly reduces stroke risk ([MDPI Foods, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/16/2619)).

**Mixed/contradictory evidence:**
- A large U.S. study published in JACC (2020) found that higher olive oil intake was associated with lower CVD risk overall, but **no significant association** was observed for total or ischemic stroke specifically. The benefit was mainly seen when olive oil replaced other fats like butter or margarine ([JACC, 2020](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2020.02.036)).
- A meta-analysis noted that while epidemiological studies generally show protective effects, results remain inconsistent ([PMC, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9623257/)).

**Bottom line:** The evidence is strongest in Mediterranean populations and when olive oil replaces less healthy fats. The stroke-specific benefit is less consistent in non-Mediterranean populations. Overall, the claim is plausible but not universally confirmed across all populations.
